svg.title: E-commerce on Azure: flash sale traffic spike
svg.text: What breaks first when nobody planned for it
Scenario: a limited drop at 18:00 sends 20x normal traffic in 90 seconds
The trick is to make every layer say no early and cheaply, so the one thing that cannot scale fast (the order database) only sees what it can take.
30–60 s. Images and JS for a
day. Most GETs never reach a
tokens from Managed Redis at a
before. HPA on RPS, KEDA on
One counter per SKU. DECRBY is
the queue at the pace SQL can
Request rates are illustrative, for a store that normally peaks at 5k req/s.
UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = ... from 3,000 sessions. Lock waits, then timeouts, then
Carts keyed by /skuId instead of /cartId. One physical partition takes the whole drop and returns
Adding AI Search replicas can take hours. Scale the day before, not when latency alerts fire.
HPA wants 300 pods, the node pool max is 40, and the region is short on that VM size today.
A rate limit counted per socket IP throttles a whole mobile carrier NAT. Test limits with real
Scale AI Search replicas, raise Cosmos DB autoscale max RU/s, request VM quota in both
Load stock counters into Redis, warm Front Door cache for the drop pages, freeze deploys
Raise HPA minReplicas and node pool minimums, add buffer pods, switch WAF challenge on
Watch: Front Door 429/5xx by route, queue depth, SQL waits, Redis CPU, admission rate
Lower the admission rate if SQL waits climb. Never raise it past what the workers drain
Reconcile Redis stock against SQL, release reservations, scale back, write the review
